901.event_title: Edward VIII gives up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson
901.place: Fort Belvedere and London, United Kingdom
901.event: Edward VIII succeeded to the throne in January 1936 and made clear that he intended to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who had divorced twice and who the government held would not be acceptable as queen. After Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin rejected a proposed morganatic marriage, Edward signed an Instrument of Abdication on 10 December 1936, witnessed by his three brothers, and it took legal effect the next day. In a radio broadcast he said he could not carry the burden of kingship without the help and support of the woman he loved, and he married her in France in 1937.
901.explanation: A reigning monarch gave up the highest office in the land rather than give up the woman he wished to marry.
901.tie_back: The kural says those wholly given over to desire for a wife miss life's highest fruit, while those intent on their duties avoid that path; Edward chose the marriage over the crown.
901._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of personal attachment outweighing public duty, though Wallis Simpson was not yet his wife and many readers view the choice sympathetically rather than as a failing.

902.event_title: Nur Jahan's name appears on Mughal coins
902.event: The Mughal emperor Jahangir married Nur Jahan in 1611, and in the later years of his reign she took charge of many of his duties and issued farmans, or sovereign orders, in her own name. She was the only Mughal queen to have coins issued in her name, and museum and reference sources describe her as the power behind the throne while Jahangir was frequently incapacitated.
902.explanation: The emperor's wealth and authority came to be seen, even on the coinage, as directed by his wife rather than by himself.
902.tie_back: The kural says the prosperity of a man who abandons his own responsibilities to his wife becomes a public matter of shame, and Nur Jahan's coins made that transfer of agency visible across the empire.
902._accuracy_note: Closely matches the commentators' point that the wife effectively controls the husband's wealth; whether this was shameful is the kural's patriarchal judgment, and Nur Jahan is admired today as an able ruler.

903.event_title: Empress Alexandra directs Russia's government while Nicholas II is at the front
903.event: In August-September 1915 Tsar Nicholas II took personal command of the Russian army and left his wife, Empress Alexandra, in charge of internal affairs, with Grigory Rasputin as her closest adviser. Over the following months many capable ministers were dismissed and replaced in rapid succession, a pattern mocked as ministerial leapfrog, and the administration was widely discredited. By early 1917 most Russians had lost faith in the tsarist regime.
903.explanation: The tsar's deference to his wife in affairs of state damaged his standing among the very people whose support his government needed.
903.tie_back: The kural says the habit of yielding to one's wife will make a man ashamed before good people, and Nicholas's reliance on Alexandra badly hurt his reputation among Russia's leaders and public.
903._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit; historians debate how much Alexandra actually controlled appointments, and the sources show Nicholas still kept final authority.

904.event_title: Mark Antony follows Cleopatra out of the Battle of Actium
904.place: Actium, off the west coast of Greece
904.event: At the naval Battle of Actium, Mark Antony and Cleopatra's fleet fought Octavian's forces under Agrippa. During the battle Cleopatra withdrew with her Egyptian ships, and Antony broke away with a small number of ships and followed her. The rest of his fleet surrendered to Octavian, and his land army surrendered about a week later, leaving Octavian master of the Roman world.
904.explanation: One of Rome's most experienced generals abandoned his own fleet and army in mid-battle to follow his partner, and his military reputation never recovered.
904.tie_back: The kural says a man ruled by his wife will not win acclaim for his work however capable he is, and Antony's long record as a commander was overshadowed by his departure from Actium.
904._accuracy_note: A close dramatisation of capability without acclaim; his motives at that moment are not recorded, so the event field describes only his actions.

905.event_title: Emperor Gaozong's senior statesmen are removed after Wu Zetian becomes empress
905.event: In 655 the Tang emperor Gaozong had his empress Wang deposed and appointed Wu Zetian in her place, against the opposition of senior court officials who objected that she did not come from one of the great noble families. Within a few years those officials were dismissed, exiled or put to death, among them the emperor's own uncle Zhangsun Wuji, who had been one of the dynasty's leading statesmen. By 660 the empress had triumphed over all her opponents.
905.explanation: The emperor did not protect the experienced counsellors who had served his family, once they stood in the way of his wife.
905.tie_back: The kural says a man who fears his wife will be afraid even to do good to good people, and Gaozong's failure to shield his loyal elder statesmen illustrates that loss of nerve.
905._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the sources do not show that Gaozong acted from fear of Wu, and modern historians see Wu as a highly capable ruler, so the fit is partial.

906.event_title: Madame de Pompadour's influence at the court of Louis XV
906.event: Louis XV declared he would rule without a chief minister, but Britannica records that his indolence and lack of self-confidence produced a court of rival ministers and mistresses, among whom Madame de Pompadour exerted considerable influence. She helped bring her protege the Duke de Choiseul into the ministry, and in 1756 the king, prompted by her, set aside his secret foreign policy. His reign saw reverses in foreign and military affairs, and he became unpopular with his subjects.
906.explanation: A king who presided over the most splendid court in Europe came to be seen as yielding his authority to a favourite, and lost the respect of his people.
906.tie_back: The kural says that even those who live as splendidly as the gods have no real dignity if they fear the arms of a woman, and Louis XV's grandeur at Versailles did not protect his reputation.
906._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Pompadour was the king's mistress, not his wife, and the sources do not tie his unpopularity to her specifically.

907.event_title: Empress Theodora counsels Justinian to stand firm in the Nika revolt
907.event: During the Nika riots in Constantinople, the emperor Justinian's advisers urged him to flee the city. His wife, Empress Theodora, advised him to stay and defend his throne, and Justinian remained. His general Belisarius then crushed the revolt, and Justinian went on to rule for more than three decades.
907.explanation: At the decisive moment the empress showed more resolve and sense of honour than the emperor and his counsellors.
907.tie_back: The kural says the dignity of a woman of honour is worthier than the manhood of a man who has lost his own, and Theodora's firmness outshone the counsel to flee.
907._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a woman's worth exceeding a wavering man's, but Justinian was not running errands for his wife; the suppression of the riot was also very bloody, so details are kept brief.

908.event_title: Edward IV's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville
908.event: While his chief supporter, Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was negotiating a marriage for him with a French princess to secure an alliance with France, Edward IV secretly married Elizabeth Woodville, a young widow of no great rank, and disclosed the marriage later in 1464. The Woodville family then rose into positions of trust near the king, further estranging Warwick. The rift widened until Warwick turned against Edward and in 1470 drove him from the throne.
908.explanation: The king's marriage cut across the plans and interests of the ally who had done most to put him on the throne, and the friendship never recovered.
908.tie_back: The kural says those who live only as their wife wishes will not meet the needs of their friends, and Edward's marriage and favour to his wife's family cost him his greatest friend.
908._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for neglecting a friend's needs; the marriage itself was Edward's own choice, not a wife's command.

909.event_title: Emperor Xuanzong loses his capital, his throne and Yang Guifei
909.event: Late in his long reign the Tang emperor Xuanzong withdrew increasingly from government and came under the influence of his consort Yang Guifei, whose relatives dominated the court. When the An Lushan rebellion took Chang'an in 756, the emperor fled toward Sichuan, and at Mawei his mutinous escort killed members of the Yang faction and demanded Yang Guifei's death, which he was unable to refuse. He then abdicated in favour of his son.
909.explanation: An emperor who had once presided over a golden age lost his government, his capital and in the end the woman he loved.
909.tie_back: The kural says those who do whatever their wives command lose virtue, wealth and even pleasure, and Xuanzong lost all three in a single year.
909._accuracy_note: A strong match to the kural's threefold loss, though Yang Guifei was a consort rather than the empress, and the rebellion had causes beyond the emperor's infatuation.

910.event_title: Titus sends Queen Berenice away from Rome
910.event: Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, lived openly with Berenice, sister of the Judean king Agrippa II, who hoped to become his wife, but the relationship was unpopular in Rome. Not daring to marry her, he sent her away, probably on his accession as emperor in 79 CE. The Roman biographer Suetonius records that he sent her from Rome at once, against her will and his own.
910.explanation: On taking power, Titus placed the duties of his office and public confidence above his personal attachment.
910.tie_back: The kural says those whose minds are joined to careful thought will not fall into the folly of being ruled by attachment to a woman, and Titus made exactly that choice when he became emperor.
910._accuracy_note: A close illustration of reason prevailing over attachment; the exact timing of her dismissal varies slightly between sources.
